name: Palate expanders (adult)

lead: Palate expanders widen the upper jaw. In adults, miniscrew-assisted (MARPE) or surgically assisted versions are used for a narrow upper jaw, and looksmaxxers discuss them for midface width and breathing.
Trials show skeletal expansion in selected patients, but reviews call efficacy evidence limited and trials rarely measure facial attractiveness.

paras: A screw-driven appliance is anchored to the teeth, mini-implants in the palate, or both, and turned to separate the midpalatal suture so bone forms in the gap. Adults often need bone anchorage or surgical help because the suture has matured.

Reported effects include pain, speech changes, a gap between front teeth, tongue sores, periodontal changes and variable success in adults. Treatment is delivered by orthodontists, and surgical versions carry operative risks.

lead: Palate expanders are orthodontic devices that widen the upper jaw (maxilla) so that upper and lower teeth fit together better. They are most often used in children and adolescents, and adult versions, such as miniscrew-assisted rapid palatal expansion (MARPE) and surgically assisted expansion, are used for transverse maxillary deficiency in patients whose palatal suture has matured [1][2].

In looksmaxxing communities, adult MARPE is discussed as a way to widen the midface, broaden the smile and improve breathing, and some users seek it for aesthetic reasons [3]. Systematic reviews describe the evidence for MARPE in late adolescents and adults as limited, while trials report skeletal expansion and some airway changes in selected patients [4][5][2].
infobox: Children and adolescents; adults for transverse maxillary deficiency
Orthodontists, with oral and maxillofacial surgeons for surgical variants
Moderate for expansion; limited for appearance

paras: Rapid palatal expansion uses a screw turned over days or weeks to widen the arch, followed by months of retention while bone fills the midline gap [1]. Slow expansion uses weekly adjustments [1]. MARPE anchors the appliance to the palate with two to four mini-implants, which allows expansion in some young adults with fused sutures and gives more skeletal and less dental change than tooth-borne devices [1][6]. Surgically assisted expansion (SARPE) involves a surgeon cutting the midpalatal suture before the expander is activated, and is used when the palate has matured [1]. One encyclopedia article states that most adults, and men in particular, may need a surgical assist for consistent results [1].

Palatal expansion was first described in the nineteenth century: Emerson Angell published a report in Dental Cosmos in 1860, and later developers included the Haas expander (reintroduced in the US in 1956) and the Hyrax expander (1968) [1]. Mini-implant-supported designs emerged in the 2010s and are the subject of a growing body of clinical literature [4][5][7].

A 2021 systematic review and meta-analysis of MARPE in patients aged 16 and older assessed success rate, skeletal and dental expansion, treatment duration and side effects, and described the evidence on efficacy as limited [4]. An umbrella review of MARPE and a 2023 update on expansion in nongrowing patients compare conventional, surgical and miniscrew-assisted approaches [5][2].

A randomized trial of 40 adolescents and young adults compared conventional rapid expansion with MARPE using low-dose CBCT to assess skeletal, alveolar and periodontal effects [6]. A multicenter controlled trial examined MARPE in adults with obstructive sleep apnea and quality of life [7]. Further randomized trials have compared MARPE with tooth-borne expansion during the post-pubertal growth spurt, and compared nasal airflow and skeletal changes after conventional expansion versus MARPE in late adolescents and young adults [8][9]. The studies' main outcomes are skeletal width, dental effects, airway and pain measures rather than facial attractiveness.

Reported effects of palatal expansion include speech changes and a lisp, extra saliva, pain and headaches when the screw is turned, tongue sores, a gap between the upper front teeth, and changes to bone and periodontal tissues such as bone fenestration and tooth extrusion [1]. The zygomatic buttress limits posterior expansion, so expansion tends to be greater at the front [1]. Older studies cited in the same source found that a third to a half of expansion could be lost before stabilization [1]. Research reports that MARPE can fail to open the suture in some patients, which is why success rate is an outcome in reviews [4].

Looksmax.org has many threads about palate expanders and MARPE, with users asking about age limits, outcomes and the choice between MARPE and jaw surgery. One user planning an expander said it was to help breathing while hoping it would widen the maxilla and improve appearance, and asked others for their aesthetic results [3]. Another encyclopedia article states that sustained tongue pressure is claimed by proponents to widen the upper jaw, that orthotropic practitioners use expanders under professional supervision mainly in children, and that mainstream orthodontic bodies find no credible evidence that mewing reshapes the jaw [10].
